name: Hassan Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to anything. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I drive a box truck for Hollowell Home, the furniture and appliance store out on the bypass. It's a two-man crew, me and Kofi, delivering sofas, fridges and washing machines into people's houses, usually eight to ten drops. Kofi's been doing it twelve years and he still carries the heavy end. I'm the driver, but I'm still learning how to park a truck that size on a street of terraced houses.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about life outside the truck?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent a room in a shared house on Canal Street, four of us and one bathroom. I've got about two weeks of money in the bank. In the evenings I do flat-pack assembly jobs through an app, which pays for my phone and petrol. I use AI for everything: quotes for the assembly jobs, sorting my budget, even working out the parking before a drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I still use AI every day, it just turned out to be a good tool, not a miracle. At work I'd tell Kofi he was right all along, which he'd love. Online I'd probably post a few of my favourite prompts for tradespeople.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my life stays the same, and that's not great. I'm on the lower pay band, the room is tiny, and Hollowell is the only furniture place for twenty miles, so if the delivery contract goes to a big courier, I'm stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and build the assembly side up, maybe ten jobs a week instead of five. I'd use AI to price the jobs and answer customers faster. I'd also try to save what the side jobs bring in, instead of spending it on takeaways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I want more than a room on Canal Street.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think Hollowell might lose the delivery contract?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because head office keeps talking about outsourcing to a national courier. If that happens, we'd be offered jobs with the courier on worse pay, or nothing. Kofi says they've been threatening it for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could the assembly work bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On a good week, maybe a hundred and fifty extra. That's the difference between two weeks' savings and two months'. I've already got AI writing my replies to customers so I don't lose them while I'm driving.

I'd post my favourite **prompts for tradespeople** online.
Kofi would hear that **he was right** all along.
think: My life stays the same, and that's **not great**.
If Hollowell **outsources deliveries**, I'm stuck with no other firm nearby.
do: Grow the **assembly side jobs** to ten a week.
Use AI to **price jobs** and answer customers faster.
**Save** the side income instead of spending it on takeaways.
feel: **Fine** but **restless**, wanting more than a small rented room.
S0.quote: Hollowell is the only furniture place for twenty miles, so if the delivery contract goes to a big courier, I'm stuck.
fieldNote: Already a **daily AI user**, so the plateau changes little.
Main worry is **outsourcing**, a business threat unrelated to AI.
Builds security through **side income**, not savings he doesn't have.

steps.text: Keep driving the Hollowell box truck with Kofi
Grow evening flat-pack assembly jobs to ten a week
Use AI to price assembly jobs and reply to customers
Save a hundred a week from assembly work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when people like me should get ahead, by learning the tools before the bosses force them. At work I'd offer to help sort the new delivery booking system. Online I'd say don't panic, get curious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my hands-on work is safe for a few years. Nobody's sending a robot up a narrow staircase with a fridge freezer yet. But the booking girls and the customer service team at Hollowell are toast, and my assembly app will start pricing jobs for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be on the team that tests the new booking system, so I know how it thinks. I'd keep building the assembly side, maybe adding small repairs. And I'd start a cheap online course in logistics planning, so I could move into the office side if a gap opens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly good, honestly. A bit sorry for the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the office staff are toast, but you'd aim for the office side. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, fair. I suppose I mean the person who runs the software, not the people it replaces. There'll be fewer office jobs, but someone has to tell it what to do when a customer's sofa won't fit through the door.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hollowell would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Brenda on the phones, who books every delivery. She's lovely to customers, but she writes everything on a paper diary. If the software takes the bookings, she's gone, and I don't think she has a backup.

I'd offer to help sort the **new booking system**.

The **booking and customer** staff at Hollowell are in trouble.

Add **small repairs** to the assembly side jobs.
Start a cheap **logistics planning course** online.
feel: **Mostly good**, a bit sorry for the office staff.
S1.quote: Nobody's sending a robot up a narrow staircase with a fridge freezer yet.
fieldNote: Admits a **contradiction**: wants the office side while saying office jobs go.
Aims to be the person who **runs the software**, not one it replaces.
Thin savings keep him uneasy even though he expects to **do well**.

steps.text: Volunteer to test Hollowell's new delivery booking system

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge, and the people who move now will be fine. I'd probably post a lot, telling drivers to learn what they can. I'm not one for blaming anyone, it's just happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, the logistics planning idea dies in 2028, because AGI does planning better than me. Then in 2031 the robots can drive and carry. I'd be 32, still renting a room, and that's tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd switch my plan to the robots themselves: getting into maintenance or setting them up in people's homes. I'd look for a short course in robotics or electrical work this year. Meanwhile I'd drive by day and do assembly by night, saving every bit I can for a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but switched on. More adrenaline than fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you think robot maintenance would still need people?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone has to unbox them, fix them when they jam, and calm down the old lady whose new robot won't work. That's people and hands for a while. I'd want to be that guy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the assembly app once robots can build flat-pack?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's gone around 2031 too, honestly. So I'd use the next few years to build up customers who know me, people who'd ring me for anything. A phone full of regular customers is worth more than any app.

say: It's **huge**, and people who move now will be fine.
I'd tell drivers to **learn what they can**.
think: The logistics planning idea dies in **2028** because AGI plans better.
By **2031** robots drive and carry, and I'm still renting a room.
do: Switch to **robot maintenance** or home set-up work.

feel: **Nervous but switched on**, more adrenaline than fear.
S2.quote: The logistics planning idea dies in 2028, because AGI does planning better than me.
fieldNote: Quickly sees that **thinking AI first** kills his office route.
Pivots to **working on the robots** rather than against them.
Plans to build a **customer base** that outlasts the assembly app.
Centre view: **blames no one**, treats it as a fact.

steps.text: Book a short robotics or electrical course this year
Build a list of regular assembly customers outside the app
Save every spare pound from evening jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get properly trained, so there's no excuse. I'd say it to Kofi too, though he'd laugh. Online I'd share any courses I found that are actually worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 35 when the robot trucks come. That's time to get a real qualification and some experience. I'd also have time to build the assembly side into a small business, maybe with a van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start an electrical apprenticeship within a year, part-time if Hollowell will let me drop a day. I'd keep using AI to run the business side: quotes, bookings, invoices. By year three I'd want a second-hand van and my own small handyman business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. Busy, but good.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two weeks' savings, how would you buy a van?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save from the side jobs for two years, then a small loan, maybe from my uncle, who's lent to my cousins before. I wouldn't touch a bank loan, the rates are mad. A three-thousand-pound van is enough to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Kofi to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi's 44, so he'd be 52 when the robots come. I'd tell Kofi, my delivery partner, to come with me and do the heavy jobs in my handyman business. He'd say no, then say yes in about four years.

think: At **35** when robot trucks come, I'd have time to qualify.
I could build the assembly side into a **small business**.

fieldNote: With five years, his mood lifts and plans turn into a **small business**.

steps.text: Start a part-time electrical apprenticeship within a year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a great run-up, and I'd mean it. I'd tell younger drivers to treat driving as a stepping stone. Online I'd be the annoying optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truly, I'd be 40 when the robot trucks come, and I'd plan to be long gone from driving by then. The thinking AI in 2036 would run my business admin, which suits me fine. My only real worry is money now, not robots later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drive for another two or three years while I finish an electrical qualification. I'd grow the assembly side into a proper handyman business with a van. By the time AGI arrives, I'd want my own customers and AI doing my paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the robots, honestly. Not calm about my bank balance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong with the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Loads. I could get injured, the van could die, or everyone else could have the same idea. But with ten years, I can fail once and try again, and that's the bit that makes me calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if Hollowell outsources the deliveries next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd go to the courier for the wage and keep the side business going. It'd be worse pay, but it'd buy me time. With ten years, that's annoying, not a disaster.

think: I'd plan to be **long gone** from driving by 40.
My real worry is **money now**, not robots later.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my office idea dies in 2028 and the robots come before I'm qualified in anything. What would help is short, cheap courses that lead straight to jobs with the robot companies, plus help getting a first van.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side jobs. Loads of drivers my age have two or three apps going. Those disappear too when the robots come, and nobody's counting them.

headlineQuote: A phone full of regular customers is worth more than any app.
portrait: Hassan, 27, drives a **furniture delivery truck** for Hollowell Home with veteran Kofi.
He rents a room, has **two weeks' savings**, and does flat-pack assembly through an app at night.
Centre-ground and practical, he **blames no one** and uses AI daily.
He pivots from office planning to **working on robots** once he sees thinking AI comes first.
With more warning he plans a **handyman business** and says he could fail once and retry.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive before he's qualified in anything.
whatWouldHelp: Short, cheap courses leading to **robot company jobs**.
Help buying a **first van** for his own business.
